items.title: Garding's inequality for a divergence-form elliptic operator
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice (CC) ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Sobolev and Lebesgue interfaces used by [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] and [[lem-elliptic-form-is-well-defined-and-bounded]]. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $L$ and its sesquilinear form $a$ be as in [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]], with ellipticity constant $\theta>0$ and coefficient bounds $M_a,M_b,M_c$. Then every $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ satisfies
$$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ \ge\ \frac{\theta}{2}\|Du\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2-\Big(\frac{nM_b^2}{2\theta}+M_c\Big)\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2,$$
and consequently, with the explicit constants $\alpha:=\theta/2$ and $\beta:=\theta/2+nM_b^2/(2\theta)+M_c$,
$$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ \ge\ \alpha\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2-\beta\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 .$$
Both inequalities restrict to $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. No Poincare inequality, no boundedness of $\Omega$ and no symmetry of $a$ is used; the constants are explicit and are not claimed to be optimal.
items.strategy: Under CC, the two cited supplier contracts apply. Split the integrand of $a(u,u)$ into its three terms. Pointwise uniform ellipticity gives $\operatorname{Re}(a^{ij}D_ju\overline{D_iu})\ge\theta|Du|^2$ a.e.; Cauchy-Schwarz and the a.e. bound $\sum_i|b^i|^2\le nM_b^2$ give $|\int b^iD_iu\overline u\,dx|\le\sqrt n\,M_b\|Du\|_2\|u\|_2$; and $|\int c|u|^2|\le M_c\|u\|_2^2$. Absorb the middle term with the scaled Young inequality $\sqrt n\,M_b\|Du\|\,\|u\|\le(\theta/2)\|Du\|^2+(nM_b^2/(2\theta))\|u\|^2$, then replace $\|Du\|_2^2$ by $\|u\|_{H^1}^2-\|u\|_2^2$. The displayed constants are the result and no sharper constant is asserted ([H] Theorem 4.21; [T] (10.47); [Si] Lecture 7 condition (C)).

items.title: A sufficiently large shift is coercive
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. In the setting of [[thm-garding-inequality-for-a-divergence-form-elliptic-operator]] put $a_\mu(u,v):=a(u,v)+\mu(u,v)_{L^2}$ for $\mu\in\mathbb R$. If $\mu\ge\beta$ with $\beta:=\theta/2+nM_b^2/(2\theta)+M_c$, then $a_\mu$ is a bounded sesquilinear form on $H^1(\Omega)$ satisfying
$$\operatorname{Re}a_\mu(u,u)\ \ge\ \frac{\theta}{2}\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2\qquad\text{for every }u\in H^1(\Omega),$$
and the same inequality holds for the restriction of $a_\mu$ to $H^1_0(\Omega)$, so $a_\mu$ is coercive with constant $\theta/2$, independent of $\mu$ once $\mu\ge\beta$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]). No boundedness of $\Omega$ is used and the shift $\mu$ is fixed.
items.strategy: Add $\mu\|u\|_2^2$ to Garding's inequality and use $\mu-\beta\ge0$. Boundedness of $a_\mu$ follows from [[lem-elliptic-form-is-well-defined-and-bounded]] plus $(u,v)_{L^2}\le\|u\|_{H^1}\|v\|_{H^1}$ ([H] proof of Theorem 4.22, printed p. 105).

items.title: The shifted elliptic solution operator
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $L,a$ be as in [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with ellipticity constant $\theta$ and coefficient bounds $M_a,M_b,M_c$, and let $\mu\ge\beta:=\theta/2+nM_b^2/(2\theta)+M_c$, so that $a_\mu=a+\mu(\cdot,\cdot)_{L^2}$ is bounded and coercive on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ with constant $\alpha:=\theta/2$ ([[cor-a-sufficiently-large-shift-is-coercive]]). For $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ the functional $F_f(v):=(f,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}$ is conjugate-linear and bounded on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ with $\|F_f\|\le\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$: Cauchy--Schwarz gives $|F_f(v)|\le\|f\|_{L^2}\|v\|_{L^2}$, and the standard $H^1_0$ norm satisfies $\|v\|_{L^2}\le\|v\|_{H^1_0}$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). The **shifted elliptic solution operator** $K_\mu$ assigns to $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ the unique $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ with $$a_\mu(u,v)=(f,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega),$$ whose existence and uniqueness are [[thm-lax-milgram]]; it is linear in $f$ with $\|K_\mu f\|_{H^1_0}\le\|f\|_{L^2}/\alpha$ ([[cor-lax-milgram-inverse-has-norm-at-most-one-over-alpha]]). $K_\mu$ is first a map $L^2(\Omega)\to H^1_0(\Omega)$; it is regarded on $L^2(\Omega)$ through the inclusion $H^1_0(\Omega)\subset L^2(\Omega)$, and the two maps are distinguished throughout. No boundedness or boundary regularity of $\Omega$ is used, and the shift is fixed and never silently changed.
items.strategy: For any open $\Omega$, apply Cauchy--Schwarz to get $|(f,v)_{L^2}|\le\|f\|_{L^2}\|v\|_{L^2}$. By the definition of the standard Sobolev norm, $\|v\|_{H^1_0}^2=\|v\|_{L^2}^2+\sum_i\|D_iv\|_{L^2}^2$, and the same inequality extends to $H^1_0$ by its closure definition; thus $\|v\|_{L^2}\le\|v\|_{H^1_0}$ and $\|F_f\|\le\|f\|_{L^2}$, without any Poincare inequality or boundedness assumption on $\Omega$. Apply [[thm-lax-milgram]] to the bounded coercive form $a_\mu$ and this bounded conjugate-linear functional. Its inverse estimate gives $\|K_\mu f\|_{H^1_0}\le\alpha^{-1}\|f\|_{L^2}$; uniqueness makes the solution map linear. Record the two realizations $L^2\to H^1_0$ and $L^2\to L^2$ through the standard inclusion. This is [H] equation (4.26), printed p. 106.

items.title: The shifted solution operator is compact on $L^2$
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited through the compact-embedding supplier named below, together with Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and **bounded**, and let $K_\mu$ be the shifted solution operator of [[def-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator]] for a fixed $\mu\ge\beta$. Then $K_\mu$, regarded as an operator on $L^2(\Omega)$, is compact: $\|K_\mu f\|_{H^1_0}\le\alpha^{-1}\|f\|_{L^2}$ ([[cor-lax-milgram-inverse-has-norm-at-most-one-over-alpha]]) and $H^1_0(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega)$ is compact ([[thm-rellich-compactness-from-w-one-p-zero-to-lp]] at $p=2$), so $K_\mu$ maps bounded subsets of $L^2(\Omega)$ to relatively compact subsets of $L^2(\Omega)$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.
items.strategy: The shifted solution map is bounded linear from $L^2(\Omega)$ to $H^1_0(\Omega)$ by the stated Lax–Milgram estimate. Apply [[cor-bounded-map-into-h-one-zero-followed-by-rellich-is-compact-on-ltwo]] to this map: its $L^2$ realization is compact because $\Omega$ is bounded and open. This is the general composition supplier applied to the elliptic solution map; the compactness proof needs no boundary regularity. The Axiom of Choice is inherited through that supplier.

items.title: On bounded domains, the unshifted equation is an identity-minus-compact equation
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $\mu\ge eta$ and let $K_\mu$ be the shifted solution operator of [[def-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator]] for the form $a$ of [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]]. For $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ and $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ the following are equivalent:
1. $a(u,v)=(f,v)_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, i.e. $u$ is a weak Dirichlet solution in the sense of [[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]];
2. $(I-\mu K_\mu)u=K_\mu f$ as elements of $L^2(\Omega)$, where $I$ is the identity of $L^2(\Omega)$.
Both sides of (2) lie in $H^1_0(\Omega)$. Thus for arbitrary open $\Omega$ the weak equation is equivalent to this identity-minus-bounded-operator equation. If $\Omega$ is bounded, also assume the Axiom of Choice; then $K_\mu$ on $L^2(\Omega)$, and hence $\mu K_\mu$, is compact by [[lem-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator-is-compact-on-ltwo]], so (2) is an identity-minus-compact Fredholm equation. The algebraic equivalence applies to the general divergence-form operator, including nonsymmetric lower-order terms.
items.strategy: Rewrite $a(u,v)=(f,v)_{L^2}$ as $a_\mu(u,v)=(f+\mu u,v)_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. By the defining uniqueness clause for $K_\mu$, this holds exactly when $u=K_\mu(f+\mu u)$ in $H^1_0$, or equivalently $(I-\mu K_\mu)u=K_\mu f$ in $L^2$. Conversely, equation (2) rearranges to that defining identity, which gives the original weak equation. Since $K_\mu:L^2\to H^1_0$, both sides of (2) belong to $H^1_0$. This algebraic equivalence uses no symmetry of $a$ and applies to the stated general lower-order coefficients. If $\Omega$ is bounded, [[lem-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator-is-compact-on-ltwo]] supplies compactness of the $L^2$ realisation, making $I-\mu K_\mu$ identity minus compact; for unbounded $\Omega$ no compactness or Fredholm claim is made. ([H] equations (4.29)-(4.30), printed pp. 107-108.)

items.title: The formal adjoint and the adjoint weak Dirichlet problem
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $L,a$ be as in [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]]. The **adjoint form** is
$$a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)},$$
a bounded sesquilinear form on $H^1(\Omega)$ with the same bound as $a$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]], [[lem-elliptic-form-is-well-defined-and-bounded]]); in coefficients
$$a^*(u,v)=\int_\Omega\Big(\overline{a^{ji}}D_ju\overline{D_iv}+\overline{b^i}u\overline{D_iv}+\overline{c}u\overline{v}\Big)dx .$$
The **formal adjoint** is the expression $L^*u:=-D_i(\overline{a^{ji}}D_ju)-D_i(\overline{b^i}u)+\overline{c}u$, understood through the identity $a^*(w,v)=\int_\Omega(L^*w)\overline v\,dx$ for smooth compactly supported $w$; the form $a^*$ is the primary object and is defined before any integration by parts. The **adjoint weak Dirichlet problem** with datum $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ asks for $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ with
$$a^*(v,w)=(f,w)_{L^2}\qquad\text{for every }w\in H^1_0(\Omega),$$
and its homogeneous version is $a^*(v,w)=0$ for all $w$. No orthogonality is invoked in this definition. Since $\operatorname{Re}a^*(u,u)=\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)$, the Garding constants of [[thm-garding-inequality-for-a-divergence-form-elliptic-operator]] also apply to $a^*$, and $a^*_\mu:=a^*+\mu(\cdot,\cdot)_{L^2}$ is coercive for $\mu\ge\beta$ ([[cor-a-sufficiently-large-shift-is-coercive]]).

**Conventions recorded with the definition.** All pairings are the $L^2$ or $H^1_0$ pairings of the cited items, with conjugation in the second slot; the datum $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ acts through the conjugate-linear functional $w\mapsto(f,w)_{L^2}$, which is an element of $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ by the Cauchy--Schwarz estimate $\|w\|_{L^2}\le\|w\|_{H^1_0}$ ([[def-h-minus-one-as-the-dual-of-h-one-zero]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). The formal expression $L^*$ is recorded as the operator whose weak pairing reproduces $a^*$ on smooth compactly supported functions; $L^*$ is not claimed to be of the same divergence form as $L$, and no boundary condition is attached to it beyond the test class $H^1_0(\Omega)$. The adjoint weak problem is stated for $H^1_0$ test functions exactly as in [[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]], and no existence or uniqueness is asserted here.
items.strategy: Define $a^*$ by conjugating the arguments of $a$ and record the coefficient formula by re-indexing the principal term; the identity $\operatorname{Re}a^*(u,u)=\operatorname{Re}\overline{a(u,u)}=\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)$ transfers Garding and the shift. The formal expression $L^*$ is recorded as the operator whose weak pairing reproduces $a^*$ on smooth compactly supported functions; it is not claimed to be in the same divergence form as $L$ ([H] Section 4.9, printed p. 107).

items.title: The adjoint solution operator solves the adjoint form problem
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\mu\ge\beta$, and let $a^*$ be the adjoint form of [[def-formal-adjoint-and-adjoint-weak-dirichlet-problem]]. Define $K^*_\mu f$, for $f\in L^2(\Omega)$, to be the unique $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ with $a^*_\mu(v,w)=(f,w)_{L^2}$ for every $w\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ (existence and uniqueness by [[thm-lax-milgram]]). Then $K^*_\mu$ is well defined and linear on $L^2(\Omega)$, and it is the Hilbert-space adjoint of the shifted solution operator $K_\mu$ of [[def-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator]]:
$$(K_\mu f,g)_{L^2}=(f,K^*_\mu g)_{L^2}\qquad\text{for all }f,g\in L^2(\Omega).$$
If $\Omega$ is bounded then $K^*_\mu$ is compact on $L^2(\Omega)$ ([[lem-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator-is-compact-on-ltwo]] applies verbatim to $a^*$). Moreover, for $v\in L^2(\Omega)$ one has $v\in\ker(I-\mu K^*_\mu)$ if and only if $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ and $a^*(v,w)=0$ for every $w\in H^1_0(\Omega)$.
items.strategy: Coercivity of $a^*_\mu$ with the same constant gives $K^*_\mu$ by Lax-Milgram. The adjoint identity is the two-line computation $(K_\mu f,g)_{L^2}=\overline{(g,K_\mu f)_{L^2}}=a^*_\mu(K^*_\mu g,K_\mu f)=(f,K^*_\mu g)_{L^2}$ (Hunter Theorem 4.23). Compactness repeats the bounded-map-into-$H^1_0$-followed-by-Rellich composition. For the kernel: $v=\mu K^*_\mu v$ is equivalent to $a^*_\mu(v,w)=\mu(v,w)_{L^2}$ for all $w$, i.e. to $a^*(v,w)=0$; conversely the latter gives $K^*_\mu(\mu v)=v$.

items.title: The elliptic Fredholm range condition is orthogonality to the adjoint kernel
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be bounded open, $\mu\ge\beta$, and let $K_\mu,K^*_\mu$ be as in [[lem-adjoint-of-the-shifted-solution-operator-solves-the-adjoint-form-problem]]. For $f\in L^2(\Omega)$,
$$K_\mu f\in\operatorname{ran}(I-\mu K_\mu)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (f,v)_{L^2}=0\ \text{ for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega)\text{ with }a^*(v,w)=0\ \forall w\in H^1_0(\Omega),$$
where $a^*$ is the adjoint form of [[def-formal-adjoint-and-adjoint-weak-dirichlet-problem]] and $K_\mu$ is the shifted solution operator of [[def-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator]].
items.strategy: Apply part 2 of [[thm-fredholm-alternative-for-identity-minus-compact]] to $A=I-\mu K_\mu$ on the Banach space $L^2(\Omega)$: $K_\mu f$ lies in the range exactly when every element of $\ker A^{\!*}$ annihilates it, where $A^{\!*}$ is the transpose on the dual. Under the Riesz identification of the dual of $L^2$ with $L^2$ the transpose kernel is $\ker(I-\mu K^*_\mu)$, and for $v$ in that kernel $(K_\mu f,v)_{L^2}=(f,K^*_\mu v)_{L^2}=(f,v/\mu)_{L^2}$, which vanishes exactly when $(f,v)_{L^2}$ does since $\mu\ne0$; finally the kernel is the weak adjoint kernel by [[lem-adjoint-of-the-shifted-solution-operator-solves-the-adjoint-form-problem]] ([H] proof of Theorem 4.24, condition (4.31), printed pp. 107-108).

items.title: The Fredholm alternative for weak elliptic Dirichlet problems
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be bounded open, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $L,a$ be as in [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with ellipticity constant $\theta$ and coefficient bounds $M_a,M_b,M_c$. Let $a^*$ be the adjoint form of [[def-formal-adjoint-and-adjoint-weak-dirichlet-problem]]. Consider the weak Dirichlet problem $a(u,v)=(f,v)_{L^2}$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, with datum $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ ([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]). Then exactly one of the following alternatives holds.
(1) The homogeneous problem $a(u,v)=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ has only the solution $u=0$. Then for every $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ the problem has exactly one weak solution $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$.
(2) The homogeneous problem has a nonzero solution. Then both homogeneous solution spaces
$$N:=\{u\in H^1_0(\Omega):a(u,v)=0\ \forall v\},\qquad N^*:=\{v\in H^1_0(\Omega):a^*(v,w)=0\ \forall w\}$$
are finite-dimensional and nontrivial with $\dim N=\dim N^*$; for $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ the problem has a solution if and only if $(f,v)_{L^2}=0$ for every $v\in N^*$; and whenever a solution exists the solution set is an affine translate of $N$, so uniqueness fails.
The data class is $L^2(\Omega)$; the weaker class $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ is deliberately not treated here.
items.strategy: Translate the abstract alternative for $A=I-\mu K_\mu$ on $L^2(\Omega)$ through [[lem-unshifted-elliptic-equation-is-an-identity-minus-compact-equation]]: weak solutions of the Dirichlet problem correspond to solutions of $Au=K_\mu f$, the weak homogeneous space $N$ is $\ker A$, and $N^*$ is $\ker A^{\!*}$ under the Riesz identification. Claim 1 of the abstract alternative gives the injective/surjective dichotomy; claim 2 gives the solvability condition, which becomes orthogonality to $N^*$ by [[lem-elliptic-fredholm-range-condition-translates-to-adjoint-kernel-orthogonality]]; claim 3 gives finite dimension and equality of dimensions. The statement names $L^2$ data explicitly because the operator reduction uses $K_\mu$ on $L^2$ ([H] Theorem 4.24, printed pp. 107-108; [L] Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1, printed pp. 101-104).

items.title: The elliptic kernel and cokernel are finite dimensional
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. In the setting of [[thm-fredholm-alternative-for-weak-elliptic-dirichlet-problems]] the weak homogeneous space $N=\{u\in H^1_0(\Omega):a(u,v)=0\ \forall v\}$ and the weak adjoint space $N^*=\{v\in H^1_0(\Omega):a^*(v,w)=0\ \forall w\}$ are finite-dimensional over $\mathbb K$ with $\dim N=\dim N^*$. Explicitly $N=\ker(I-\mu K_\mu)$ and $N^*=\ker(I-\mu K^*_\mu)$ as subspaces of $L^2(\Omega)$ ([[lem-unshifted-elliptic-equation-is-an-identity-minus-compact-equation]], [[lem-adjoint-of-the-shifted-solution-operator-solves-the-adjoint-form-problem]]), so this common dimension is the **geometric multiplicity**, meaning the dimension of the eigenspace $E_1(T)=\ker(T-I)$ ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), of eigenvalue $1$ for each compact operator $T=\mu K_\mu$ and $T=\mu K^*_\mu$. No equality of algebraic multiplicities is asserted. The common geometric multiplicity is independent of the admissible shift $\mu\ge\beta$.
items.strategy: Identify the weak kernels with ker(I−mu K_mu) and ker(I−mu K*_mu). The abstract Fredholm alternative equates their finite dimensions through the cokernel/annihilator identification. Each dimension is the geometric multiplicity (dimension of the eigenspace) of eigenvalue 1 for its compact solution operator, and the weak spaces show this geometric multiplicity is shift-independent; no algebraic-multiplicity claim is made.

items.title: Uniqueness implies existence for the elliptic Dirichlet problem
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. In the setting of [[thm-fredholm-alternative-for-weak-elliptic-dirichlet-problems]] suppose both homogeneous problems are trivial: $a(u,v)=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ implies $u=0$, and $a^*(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ implies $v=0$ (the two conditions are equivalent by the finite dimension and equality of dimensions in [[cor-elliptic-kernel-and-cokernel-are-finite-dimensional]]). Then for every $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ there is exactly one $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ with $a(u,v)=(f,v)_{L^2}$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. Moreover the solution map $f\mapsto u$ is a bounded linear operator from $L^2(\Omega)$ to $H^1_0(\Omega)$: explicitly $u=K_\mu(I-\mu K_\mu)^{-1}f$ for every admissible $\mu\ge\beta$, with $(I-\mu K_\mu)^{-1}$ bounded on $L^2(\Omega)$ ([[def-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator]], [[lem-neumann-series-and-small-perturbations-of-bounded-inverses]]).
items.strategy: The triviality of both homogeneous problems excludes alternative (2) of the Fredholm alternative, so alternative (1) grants existence and uniqueness for every $L^2$ datum. For the operator bound, the abstract alternative also gives bounded invertibility of $I-\mu K_\mu$ when it is injective, and $u=K_\mu(I-\mu K_\mu)^{-1}f$ follows from the identity-minus-compact reduction; the compact perturbation of the identity with trivial kernel has a bounded inverse ([H] Theorem 4.24(1), printed p. 107; claim 1 of [[thm-fredholm-alternative-for-identity-minus-compact]]).

items.title: Smooth compactly supported functions of an open set are dense in L2
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.
items.strategy: Given $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ extend it by zero to $F\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$. The exhaustion $K_m:=\{x\in\Omega:|x|\le m,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)\ge1/m\}$ (a canonical sequence of compact subsets of $\Omega$ with $\bigcup_mK_m=\Omega$) makes $F_m:=\mathbf 1_{K_m}F\to F$ in $L^2$ by dominated convergence. Choose $m$ with $\|F-F_m\|_2<\delta/2$. Choose a smooth bump $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;[0,1])$ with $\chi=1$ on $K_m$; then $G:=\chi F$ is supported in a compact subset of $\Omega$ and $\|F-G\|_2\le\|F-F_m\|_2<\delta/2$ because $0\le\chi\le1$. Mollify $G$ at scale $\eta$ smaller than half the distance from $\operatorname{supp}\chi$ to $\partial\Omega$: the mollified class $G_\eta$ is smooth, compactly supported in $\Omega$, and $\|G_\eta-G\|_2\to0$ by the approximate-identity theorem; choose $\eta$ with $\|G_\eta-G\|_2<\delta/2$. Then $\varphi:=G_\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Since $C_c^\infty(\Omega)\subseteq H^1_0(\Omega)$ by definition of the closure, $H^1_0$ is dense in $L^2$, and the vanishing-against-$H^1_0$ statement follows. The argument is the standard exhaustion-mollification density proof for an arbitrary open set, with everything expressed in the library's class conventions.

items.title: The $L^2$ operator associated with a symmetric elliptic form
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. **Symmetric case.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $a$ be the divergence-form sesquilinear form of [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with $b^i\equiv0$, coefficients satisfying $a^{ij}=\overline{a^{ji}}$ a.e. and real $c$, all measurable and essentially bounded, and with uniform ellipticity constant $\theta$. Thus $a(u,v)=\int_\Omega(a^{ij}D_ju\overline{D_iv}+cu\overline v)\,dx$ is a bounded symmetric form, $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]], [[def-formal-adjoint-and-adjoint-weak-dirichlet-problem]]). Define
$$D(L):=\Big\{u\in H^1_0(\Omega):\ \exists f\in L^2(\Omega)\text{ with }a(u,v)=(f,v)_{L^2}\ \forall v\in H^1_0(\Omega)\Big\},\qquad Lu:=f .$$
This is well defined: if $f,g$ both satisfy the defining identity then $(f-g,v)_{L^2}=0$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, and $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$ ([[lem-smooth-compactly-supported-functions-are-dense-in-ltwo-of-an-open-set]]), so $f=g$ in $L^2(\Omega)$. The space $D(L)$ is a linear subspace of $H^1_0(\Omega)$ containing the range of every shifted solution operator ([[def-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator]]), and $L:D(L)\to L^2(\Omega)$ is linear. With only bounded measurable coefficient hypotheses, $D(L)$ may be a proper subspace of the form domain $H^1_0(\Omega)$; those hypotheses alone do not assert $C_c^\infty(\Omega)\subseteq D(L)$. Membership $u\in D(L)$ with $Lu=f$ is exactly the weak statement of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values in $L^2$ data ([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]).

**Well-definedness and symmetry, recorded with the definition.** Boundedness of $a$ on $H^1(\Omega)$ is [[lem-elliptic-form-is-well-defined-and-bounded]] with $b=0$, and symmetry follows by conjugating the defining integrand: with $a^{ij}=\overline{a^{ji}}$ and $c$ real, $\overline{a(v,u)}=\int_\Omega\bigl(\overline{a^{ji}}D_ju\overline{D_iv}+\overline c\,\overline v u\bigr)dx=a(u,v)$ after re-indexing. Hence the pair $a,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{L^2}$ is the symmetric sesquilinear pair whose weak identity defines $D(L)$. The representing datum is unique by the density argument above, so $Lu$ is a well-defined class; linearity of $L$ follows from linearity of $a$ and of the $L^2$ pairing. The range inclusion $\operatorname{ran}K_\mu\subseteq D(L)$ holds because $K_\mu g$ satisfies $a(K_\mu g,v)=a_\mu(K_\mu g,v)-\mu(K_\mu g,v)_{L^2}=(g-\mu K_\mu g,v)_{L^2}$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, with datum $g-\mu K_\mu g\in L^2(\Omega)$ ([[def-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-countable-choice]]). No claim of self-adjointness, closedness, density of $D(L)$, or identification with a classical differential expression is made here; those belong to the following items.
items.strategy: Fix the coefficient symmetry $a^{ij}=\overline{a^{ji}}$, $b=0$, $c$ real, so that $a$ is Hermitian. Define the operator through the weak identity with an $L^2$ datum and prove uniqueness of the representing $f$ by density of $H^1_0$ in $L^2$, using the local density lemma constructed on this page. The domain $D(L)$ is defined by $L^2$ representability and may be a proper subspace of the form domain; the bare measurable-coefficient hypotheses do not assert $C_c^\infty(\Omega)\subseteq D(L)$ ([H] Section 4.8, printed p. 106; [L] Chapter 4 Section 4.3, printed pp. 94-98).

items.title: The associated elliptic operator is densely defined, symmetric and lower bounded
items.strategy: Range inclusion: for $f\in L^2$, testing the definition of $K_\mu f$ gives $a(K_\mu f,v)=(f-\mu K_\mu f,v)_{L^2}$ for all $v$, so $K_\mu f\in D(L)$ and $L(K_\mu f)=f-\mu K_\mu f$. Density: if $y\in L^2$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}K_\mu$, then $a_\mu(K_\mu y,K_\mu y)=(y,K_\mu y)_{L^2}=0$, so coercivity forces $K_\mu y=0$; then $(y,v)_{L^2}=a_\mu(0,v)=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0$ and density of $H^1_0$ in $L^2$ gives $y=0$, so $\operatorname{ran}K_\mu$ is dense by the double-orthogonal-complement theorem. Symmetry: if $Lu=f$ and $Lv=g$, then $(Lu,v)_{L^2}=a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}=\overline{(Lv,u)_{L^2}}=(u,Lv)_{L^2}$. Lower bound: Garding's inequality. All three properties are proved from the form and the definitions, not assumed from the differential expression ([H] Section 4.8, printed p. 106; [L] Chapter 4 Section 4.1, printed pp. 84-86).

items.title: The symmetric elliptic form operator is self-adjoint with compact resolvent
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice, together with the Axiom of Choice where the compactness clause is used. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $L,D(L)$ be the symmetric-case operator of [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]], with $D(L)$ dense and $L$ symmetric and lower bounded ([[lem-associated-elliptic-operator-is-densely-defined-symmetric-and-lower-bounded]]); let its scalar field be $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and fix $\mu\ge\beta$. Then $L$ is self-adjoint: $L=L^*$, the adjoint being taken in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for the densely defined operator $L$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Moreover $L+\mu:D(L)\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a bijection with inverse $K_\mu$. If $\Omega$ is bounded and the Axiom of Choice holds, then $K_\mu$ is compact ([[lem-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator-is-compact-on-ltwo]]). For $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, $L$ has compact resolvent: $(L-\lambda)^{-1}$ is compact on $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ for every $\lambda$ in the resolvent set of $L$ ([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). For $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$, identify $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ canonically with $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)_{\mathbb C}$ by $u+iv\leftrightarrow(u,v)$, and let $L_{\mathbb C}(u+iv):=Lu+iLv$ on $D(L_{\mathbb C})=D(L)+iD(L)$ ([[def-complexification-of-a-real-vector-space]], [[def-complexification-of-a-real-linear-map]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Then $L_{\mathbb C}$ is self-adjoint and has compact resolvent: $(L_{\mathbb C}-\lambda)^{-1}$ is compact on $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ for every $\lambda$ in its resolvent set ([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]).
items.strategy: Surjectivity of L+mu comes from the shifted solution operator. In the complex case, Lax–Milgram gives both nonreal ranges and the range criterion gives self-adjointness. In the real case, full range proves real self-adjointness; the canonical Hilbert isometry L2_R_C ≅ L2_C sends u+iv to its real/imaginary components, and testing the adjoint identity on real vectors proves the complexified operator is self-adjoint. When Ω is bounded, K_mu is compact; its real complexification is compact by extracting convergent subsequences of the real and imaginary images. For either complex realization L~, K~=(L~+mu)^−1. For λ in its resolvent, the two resolvent identities Rλ−K~=cRλK~=cK~Rλ make I−cK~ invertible with inverse I+cRλ, so Rλ=(I+cRλ)K~ is compact.

items.title: Symmetric elliptic weak eigenpairs
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. In the symmetric case of [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]], a **weak eigenpair** of the Dirichlet problem for $L$ is a pair $(\lambda,u)$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)\setminus\{0\}$ and
$$a(u,v)=\lambda(u,v)_{L^2}\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega);$$
$\lambda$ is a **weak eigenvalue** and $u$ a **weak eigenfunction**. The eigenspace $E_\lambda:=\{u\in H^1_0(\Omega):a(u,v)=\lambda(u,v)_{L^2}\ \forall v\}$ is a closed linear subspace. Weak eigenpairs are exactly operator eigenpairs: $(\lambda,u)$ is a weak eigenpair if and only if $u\in D(L)\setminus\{0\}$ and $Lu=\lambda u$ ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]], [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]]). Eigenfunctions are $L^2$ equivalence classes; no canonical representative or canonical vector in a multiple eigenspace is selected. The **multiplicity** of $\lambda$ is $\dim E_\lambda$, with no finiteness assertion for general open $\Omega$.

**Well-definedness, recorded with the definition.** $E_\lambda$ is a linear subspace because $a$ and the $L^2$ pairing are linear in the first argument; it is closed in $H^1_0(\Omega)$ because both $u\mapsto a(u,v)$ and $u\mapsto(u,v)_{L^2}$ are continuous on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ for each fixed $v$: boundedness of $a$ and the estimate $|(u,v)_{L^2}|\le\|u\|_{L^2}\|v\|_{L^2}\le\|u\|_{H^1_0}\|v\|_{H^1_0}$ show that weak limits of vectors in $E_\lambda$ remain in $E_\lambda$. The equivalence with operator eigenpairs is the definition of $D(L)$ and $Lu$: the weak identity for $(\lambda,u)$ says exactly that the datum $f=\lambda u$ represents $a(u,\cdot)$ on $H^1_0(\Omega)$, which, together with $u\ne0$, is the pair of conditions $u\in D(L)\setminus\{0\}$ and $Lu=\lambda u$. The eigenvalue $\lambda$ is required to be real, as is forced for the symmetric form once $u\ne0$: taking $v=u$ gives $\lambda\|u\|_{L^2}^2=a(u,u)=\overline{a(u,u)}$. All equalities are equalities of $L^2$ and $H^1_0$ classes ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]], [[def-countable-choice]]); no regularity of eigenfunctions and no boundary values beyond membership in $H^1_0$ are asserted.
items.strategy: Define weak eigenpairs by the variational equation and identify them with operator eigenpairs through D(L). Prove Eλ is closed by continuity of the form and L² pairing, require λ real as forced by symmetry, and define multiplicity as dim Eλ without claiming it is finite for arbitrary open Ω. The real and complex scalar conventions remain explicit.

items.title: The symmetric shifted solution operator is positive and self-adjoint
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. In the symmetric case of [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]], with $\Omega$ open and $\mu\ge\beta$, the shifted solution operator $K_\mu$ of [[def-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator]], regarded on $L^2(\Omega)$, is self-adjoint and positive:
$$(K_\mu f,g)_{L^2}=(f,K_\mu g)_{L^2},\qquad (K_\mu f,f)_{L^2}=a_\mu(K_\mu f,K_\mu f)\ \ge\ \alpha\|K_\mu f\|_{H^1_0}^2\ \ge\ 0$$
for all $f,g\in L^2(\Omega)$, with $(K_\mu f,f)_{L^2}=0$ if and only if $f=0$; in particular $K_\mu$ is injective. Moreover $a(K_\mu f,v)=(f-\mu K_\mu f,v)_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, so $K_\mu f\in D(L)$ and $L(K_\mu f)=f-\mu K_\mu f$. Symmetry of $K_\mu$ is verified from the form; no self-adjointness of the differential expression is assumed.
items.strategy: For $f,g\in L^2$ use the defining identity twice: $(K_\mu f,g)_{L^2}=\overline{(g,K_\mu f)_{L^2}}=\overline{a_\mu(K_\mu g,K_\mu f)}=a_\mu(K_\mu f,K_\mu g)=(f,K_\mu g)_{L^2}$, where symmetry of $a_\mu$ is used in the middle step. Positivity is $a_\mu(K_\mu f,K_\mu f)\ge\alpha\|K_\mu f\|_{H^1_0}^2$; if it vanishes then $K_\mu f=0$, hence $(f,v)_{L^2}=a_\mu(0,v)=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0$ and density of $H^1_0$ in $L^2$ gives $f=0$. The range description is the computation already used for density in [[lem-associated-elliptic-operator-is-densely-defined-symmetric-and-lower-bounded]] ([L] Chapter 4 Section 4.1, printed pp. 85-86).

items.title: Discrete spectrum of a symmetric elliptic Dirichlet operator
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. In the symmetric case of [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]], let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, open and bounded, fix $\mu\ge\beta$, and let $K_\mu$ be the shifted solution operator of [[def-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator]] ([[lem-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator-is-compact-on-ltwo]]). Then the following hold.
1. There are real numbers $\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots$ with $\lambda_j\to+\infty$, each eigenvalue repeated according to its finite multiplicity, and an orthonormal basis $\{e_j\}_{j\ge1}$ of $L^2(\Omega)$ with $e_j\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ and
$$a(e_j,v)=\lambda_j(e_j,v)_{L^2}\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega),$$
equivalently $e_j\in D(L)$ and $Le_j=\lambda_je_j$ in the sense of [[def-symmetric-elliptic-weak-eigenpair]]. Explicitly $\lambda_j=\nu_j^{-1}-\mu$, where $\nu_j>0$, $\nu_j\downarrow0$, are the nonzero eigenvalues of the compact self-adjoint positive operator $K_\mu$ with $K_\mu e_j=\nu_je_j$ ([[lem-symmetric-shifted-solution-operator-is-positive-and-self-adjoint]]).
2. Every weak eigenvalue of the Dirichlet problem occurs in the list, and each listed $\lambda_j$ is a weak eigenvalue with finite-dimensional eigenspace; eigenspaces belonging to distinct eigenvalues are $L^2$-orthogonal.
3. $\lambda_j>-\mu$ for every $j$, and $a(u,u)\ge-\beta\|u\|^2_{L^2}$ for every $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$.
The proof applies the compact self-adjoint spectral theorem once to $K_\mu$; since $\ker K_\mu=\{0\}$, no Hilbert basis of the kernel is ever selected, and the union of orthonormal bases of the nonzero eigenspaces of $K_\mu$ is already a Hilbert basis of $L^2(\Omega)$.
items.strategy:
Apply [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]] to $K_\mu$: its nonzero eigenvalues $
u_j$ are real, have finite multiplicity, satisfy $
u_j\downarrow0$, and orthonormal bases of its nonzero eigenspaces form a complete orthonormal family with closed span $(\ker K_\mu)^\perp$; $\ker K_\mu=\{0\}$ by [[lem-symmetric-shifted-solution-operator-is-positive-and-self-adjoint]], so that family is a Hilbert basis of $L^2$. Translating $K_\mu e_j=
u_je_j$ with the defining identity gives $a(e_j,v)=(
u_j^{-1}-\mu)(e_j,v)_{L^2}$; conversely a weak eigenvalue satisfies $K_\mu u=u/(\lambda+\mu)$, because $\lambda+\mu>0$ follows from coercivity ($0<(L+\mu)u,u)=(\lambda+\mu)\|u\|^2$), so the two lists agree. Listing the eigenvalues of $K_\mu$ in decreasing order makes $\lambda_j=
u_j^{-1}-\mu$ increasing; finite multiplicity and $\lambda_j>-\mu$ follow, and Garding gives the lower bound $- eta$ ([H] Theorem 4.25, printed pp. 108-109; [L] Corollary 4.8, printed pp. 94-96; [B] Theorem 9.31, printed p. 311).

items.title: Eigenbasis expansion in the form norm
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. In the symmetric case of [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]] with $\Omega$ nonempty bounded open, let $\{e_j\}$ and $\{\lambda_j\}$ be the eigenbasis and eigenvalues of [[thm-discrete-spectrum-of-a-symmetric-elliptic-dirichlet-operator]] and fix $\mu\ge\beta$. Then:
1. for every $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ the series $\sum_j(u,e_j)_{L^2}e_j$ converges to $u$ in the $H^1_0(\Omega)$ norm (equivalently in the inner-product norm $a_\mu$), and
$$a_\mu(u,u)=\sum_{j\ge1}(\lambda_j+\mu)\,|(u,e_j)_{L^2}|^2;$$
2. for every $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ the series $\sum_j(f,e_j)_{L^2}e_j$ converges to $f$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ and $\|f\|_{L^2}^2=\sum_j|(f,e_j)_{L^2}|^2$ (Parseval);
3. consequently $a(u,u)=\sum_j\lambda_j|(u,e_j)_{L^2}|^2$ for every $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, the series being absolutely convergent.
This expansion is the form-domain companion of the $L^2$ eigenbasis of the spectral theorem.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. In the symmetric case of [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]] with $\Omega$ nonempty bounded open, let $\{\lambda_j\}$ be the eigenvalues of [[thm-discrete-spectrum-of-a-symmetric-elliptic-dirichlet-operator]]. Then
$$\lambda_1=\min_{u\in H^1_0(\Omega)\setminus\{0\}}\frac{a(u,u)}{\|u\|_{L^2}^2},$$
the minimum is attained exactly at the nonzero elements of the eigenspace $E_{\lambda_1}$, and $\lambda_1$ is the smallest weak eigenvalue. If in addition the form $a$ is coercive on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ with constant $\alpha'>0$ (for instance when the hypotheses of [[thm-lax-milgram-solvability-for-coercive-divergence-form-equations]] hold, or $a$ is the principal Dirichlet form), then $\lambda_1\ge\alpha'>0$; in general only $\lambda_1>-\mu$ and the Garding bound $\lambda_1\ge-\beta$ are asserted.
items.strategy: For $u\ne0$ write $c_j=(u,e_j)_{L^2}$; claims 1 and 2 of [[lem-eigenbasis-expansion-in-the-form-norm]] give $\|u\|_{L^2}^2=\sum_j|c_j|^2$ and $a(u,u)=\sum_j\lambda_j|c_j|^2$, so the Rayleigh quotient is the weighted average $\sum_j\lambda_j|c_j|^2/\sum_j|c_j|^2$, which is at least $\lambda_1$ with equality exactly when $c_j=0$ for every $j$ with $\lambda_j>\lambda_1$. The eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ is attained by $e_1$, so the infimum is a minimum, and coercivity gives the positive lower bound ([LS] Chapter 9, Rayleigh principle (9.1), printed p. 51; [T] equation (10.23), printed p. 228; [Si] Lecture 10, printed pp. 101-104).

items.title: The Courant-Fischer min-max principle for elliptic eigenvalues
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. In the symmetric case of [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]] with $\Omega$ nonempty bounded open, let $\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots$ be the eigenvalues of [[thm-discrete-spectrum-of-a-symmetric-elliptic-dirichlet-operator]], repeated according to multiplicity. Then for every $k\ge1$,
$$\lambda_k=\min\Big\{\max_{u\in S\setminus\{0\}}\frac{a(u,u)}{\|u\|_{L^2}^2}:\ S\subseteq H^1_0(\Omega),\ \dim S=k\Big\}=\max\Big\{\inf_{u\in (H^1_0(\Omega)\cap T^{\perp_{L^2}})\setminus\{0\}}\frac{a(u,u)}{\|u\|_{L^2}^2}:\ T\subseteq H^1_0(\Omega),\ \dim T=k-1\Big\},$$
where $T^{\perp_{L^2}}$ is the orthogonal complement in $L^2(\Omega)$, and for $k=1$ the maximum is over $T=\{0\}$, so $H^1_0(\Omega)\cap T^{\perp_{L^2}}=H^1_0(\Omega)$. Both outer extrema are attained: the first at $S=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$, and the second at $T=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\dots,e_{k-1}\}$, where the inner infimum is attained at $e_k$. No smoothness of $\partial\Omega$ is required.
items.strategy: Use the representation of the Rayleigh quotient as the weighted average $\sum\lambda_j|c_j|^2/\sum|c_j|^2$ from [[lem-eigenbasis-expansion-in-the-form-norm]]. For min-max, $S_k=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$ gives the upper bound and rank-nullity gives the reverse bound. For max-inf, take orthogonal complements in $L^2$: $T_{k-1}=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\dots,e_{k-1}\}$ has infimum $\lambda_k$, attained at $e_k$, and every $(k-1)$-dimensional $T$ has a nonzero intersection with $\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$, whose quotient is at most $\lambda_k$. Thus the outer maximum is attained at $T_{k-1}$; no inner minimum for arbitrary $T$ is required.

items.title: The Poincare constant is the reciprocal square root of the first Dirichlet eigenvalue
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty bounded open and consider the Dirichlet Laplacian, i.e. the symmetric case with $a^{ij}=\delta^{ij}$, $b=0$, $c=0$ ([[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]]). Then its first eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda_1>0$ and $$\lambda_1=\min_{u\in H^1_0(\Omega)\setminus\{0\}}\frac{\|Du\|_{L^2}^2}{\|u\|_{L^2}^2},\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le\lambda_1^{-1/2}\|Du\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\quad(u\in H^1_0(\Omega)),$$ with equality for nonzero $u$ exactly at the nonzero first eigenfunctions; $u=0$ is also the trivial equality case. Hence $\lambda_1^{-1/2}$ is the optimal (smallest) constant in the $L^2$ zero-trace Poincare inequality on $\Omega$: every constant $C$ with $\|u\|_{L^2}\le C\|Du\|_{L^2}$ for all $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ satisfies $C\ge\lambda_1^{-1/2}$, and the positive admissible constant $C_P$ of [[thm-poincare-inequality-for-w-one-p-zero]] at $p=2$ therefore satisfies $C_P\ge\lambda_1^{-1/2}$. No numerical value or domain formula for $\lambda_1$ is asserted.
items.strategy: For the model coefficients, the Rayleigh principle identifies lambda_1 with the minimum of ||Du||_2^2/||u||_2^2. Boundedness of Omega lets the zero-trace Poincare supplier apply; choose a positive admissible C_P to obtain lambda_1>=C_P^{-2}>0. The Rayleigh minimum gives the sharp inequality, with equality for nonzero u exactly in the first eigenspace and the zero function as a separate trivial equality case. Testing any admissible constant on a nonzero first eigenfunction proves optimality; Poincare directly rules out a zero gradient, without assuming Omega connected.

items.title: Non-invertible elliptic shifts form a discrete set in the self-adjoint case
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. In the symmetric case of [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]], let the scalar field be $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $\Omega$ be nonempty, bounded and open. Write $L,D(L)$ for the symmetric-case operator. Define the complex Hilbert space $\widetilde H:=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and the complex operator $\widetilde L$ as follows: if $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, set $\widetilde L=L$; if $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$, use the canonical isometric identification $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)_{\mathbb C}\cong L^2(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and set $\widetilde L=L_{\mathbb C}$, the complexification $L_{\mathbb C}(u+iv)=Lu+iLv$ on $D(L)+iD(L)$ ([[def-complex-l-two-inner-product]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-complexification-of-a-real-vector-space]], [[def-complexification-of-a-real-linear-map]], [[thm-symmetric-elliptic-form-operator-is-self-adjoint-with-compact-resolvent]]). Let $\{\lambda_j\}$ be the eigenvalues of [[thm-discrete-spectrum-of-a-symmetric-elliptic-dirichlet-operator]], repeated according to multiplicity. For every real $\lambda$, the base-field operator $L-\lambda:D(L)\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is bijective with bounded inverse if and only if $\lambda\notin\{\lambda_j\}$. For such $\lambda$ the inverse $R_\lambda:=(L-\lambda)^{-1}$, in the adopted $L-\lambda$ convention, is given by the convergent series
$$R_\lambda f=\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{(f,e_j)_{L^2}}{\lambda_j-\lambda}\,e_j\qquad(f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)),$$
which converges in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and in $H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and $\|R_\lambda\|=1/\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\{\lambda_j\})$. In the real case this inverse complexifies to $(\widetilde L-\lambda)^{-1}$ with the same operator norm, and conversely the complex resolvent at a real $\lambda$ restricts to the real inverse. Finally, the complex spectrum is $\sigma(\widetilde L)=\{\lambda_j\}$: a closed discrete subset of $\mathbb R$, bounded below, unbounded above, with no finite accumulation point; the nonreal resolvent exclusion follows from [[thm-self-adjoint-resolvent-estimate]].
items.strategy: For lambda outside the discrete eigenvalue set, form the spectral series. The coefficient bound first gives L² convergence; claim 1 of [[lem-eigenbasis-expansion-in-the-form-norm]] gives a summable positive form-norm series, so its partial sums are Cauchy in aμ and converge strongly in H¹₀. The L² and form limits agree, and the weak eigenrelations identify (L−lambda)u=f. Injectivity follows from the eigenvalue list; Parseval gives the exact resolvent norm.

items.title: The elliptic resolvent identity
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. In the symmetric case of [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]], let the scalar field be $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $\Omega$ be bounded and open. Define $\widetilde H:=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $\widetilde L=L$ if $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$; if $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$, use the canonical isometric identification $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)_{\mathbb C}\cong L^2(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and set $\widetilde L=L_{\mathbb C}$, the complexification $L_{\mathbb C}(u+iv)=Lu+iLv$ on $D(L)+iD(L)$ ([[def-complex-l-two-inner-product]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-complexification-of-a-real-vector-space]], [[def-complexification-of-a-real-linear-map]], [[thm-symmetric-elliptic-form-operator-is-self-adjoint-with-compact-resolvent]]). Write $\sigma(\widetilde L)$ for its complex spectrum as in [[cor-noninvertible-elliptic-shifts-form-a-discrete-set-in-the-self-adjoint-case]]. For $z\notin\sigma(\widetilde L)$ put $R_z:=(\widetilde L-z)^{-1}$ in the adopted $\widetilde L-z$ convention, so that $R_z:\widetilde H\to D(\widetilde L)$ is bijective onto $D(\widetilde L)$ with $(\widetilde L-z)R_z=I$ on $\widetilde H$ and $R_z(\widetilde L-z)=I$ on $D(\widetilde L)$. Then for all $z,w\notin\sigma(\widetilde L)$
$$R_z-R_w=(z-w)R_zR_w=(z-w)R_wR_z,$$
the identities holding on all of $\widetilde H$; in particular $R_zR_w=R_wR_z$. Each $R_z$ is compact on $\widetilde H$.
items.strategy: Compute on $L^2$: $R_\lambda-R_\mu=R_\lambda(L-\mu)R_\mu-R_\lambda(L-\lambda)R_\mu=R_\lambda((L-\mu)-(L-\lambda))R_\mu=(\lambda-\mu)R_\lambda R_\mu$, using $(L-\mu)R_\mu=I$ and $R_\lambda(L-\lambda)=I$ on the appropriate domains; the products are everywhere defined because $R_\mu$ maps $L^2$ into $D(L)$. Exchanging $\lambda$ and $\mu$ gives the second displayed form and commutativity. Compactness of $R_\lambda$ is the compact-resolvent clause of [[thm-symmetric-elliptic-form-operator-is-self-adjoint-with-compact-resolvent]]; the published general identity [[lem-second-resolvent-identity-for-closed-operator-perturbations]] compares but is not needed ([Si] Lecture 10; [H] Section 4.8, printed p. 106).

items.title: Eigenfunctions for distinct symmetric elliptic eigenvalues are L2-orthogonal
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. In the symmetric case of [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]], let $(\lambda,u)$ and $(\mu,v)$ be weak eigenpairs as in [[def-symmetric-elliptic-weak-eigenpair]] with $\lambda\ne\mu$. Then $(u,v)_{L^2}=0$. If the scalar field is $\mathbb C$ and the coefficients are real, conjugation preserves weak eigenpairs at the same eigenvalue; each nonzero real or imaginary part of an eigenfunction is then a real-valued weak eigenfunction, so an eigenfunction can be chosen real.

In the complex case with real coefficients, conjugate the equation using a( ar u,w)=overline{a(u, ar w)}; the nonzero real or imaginary parts are then real-valued eigenfunctions.

items.title: Spectral series solution of an invertible symmetric elliptic problem
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. In the symmetric case of [[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]] with $\Omega$ nonempty bounded open, suppose $0$ is not an eigenvalue of $L$ (equivalently, by [[thm-discrete-spectrum-of-a-symmetric-elliptic-dirichlet-operator]], no nonzero $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ satisfies $a(u,v)=0$ for all $v$; this holds in particular when $a$ is coercive on $H^1_0(\Omega)$). Then $L:D(L)\to L^2(\Omega)$ is bijective, and for every $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ the unique weak solution $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ of $a(u,v)=(f,v)_{L^2}$ for all $v$ is
$$u=L^{-1}f=\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{(f,e_j)_{L^2}}{\lambda_j}\,e_j,$$
the series converging in $L^2(\Omega)$ and in $H^1_0(\Omega)$; moreover $u\in D(L)$ with $Lu=f$ and $\|u\|_{L^2}\le\big(\min_j|\lambda_j|\big)^{-1}\|f\|_{L^2}$ (and $\|u\|_{L^2}\le\lambda_1^{-1}\|f\|_{L^2}$ when $\lambda_1>0$, in particular under coercivity of $a$).
items.strategy: Injectivity of $L$ is the hypothesis that $0$ is not an eigenvalue; surjectivity is the resolvent formula of [[cor-noninvertible-elliptic-shifts-form-a-discrete-set-in-the-self-adjoint-case]] at $\lambda=0$, which provides the displayed series and the convergence. For convergence in $L^2$: $\sum_j|(f,e_j)|^2\lambda_j^{-2}\le\delta^{-2}\|f\|^2$ with $\delta=\min_j|\lambda_j|>0$, positive because $\lambda_j\to+\infty$. For convergence in $H^1_0$ and membership $u\in D(L)$: claim 1 of [[lem-eigenbasis-expansion-in-the-form-norm]] applied to the weighted series, whose $a_\mu$-sum is $\sum_j(\lambda_j+\mu)|(f,e_j)|^2\lambda_j^{-2}\le C\|f\|^2$ with $C=\sup_j(\lambda_j+\mu)\lambda_j^{-2}<\infty$; then $a(u,v)=\sum_j(f,e_j)(e_j,v)=(f,v)$ for all $v$. The $L^2$ bounds are immediate ([H] end of Section 4.10, printed pp. 109-110).

items.title: The first Dirichlet eigenvalue is monotone under domain inclusion
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega_1\subseteq\Omega_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty bounded open sets, let $a^{ij}$ be measurable, essentially bounded and uniformly elliptic on $\Omega_2$ with $a^{ij}=\overline{a^{ji}}$, and for $i=1,2$ let $a^{(i)}$ be the principal Dirichlet form $a^{(i)}(u,v)=\int_{\Omega_i}a^{ij}D_ju\overline{D_iv}\,dx$ on $H^1_0(\Omega_i)$; the model case $a^{ij}=\delta^{ij}$ is the Dirichlet Laplacian. Let $\lambda_k(\Omega_i)$ be the eigenvalues of the corresponding symmetric elliptic Dirichlet operator ([[thm-discrete-spectrum-of-a-symmetric-elliptic-dirichlet-operator]]) . Then
$$\lambda_k(\Omega_2)\le\lambda_k(\Omega_1)\qquad\text{for every }k\ge1,$$
in particular $\lambda_1(\Omega_2)\le\lambda_1(\Omega_1)$: making the domain smaller raises the Dirichlet frequencies. The mechanism is that extension by zero maps $H^1_0(\Omega_1)$ isometrically into $H^1_0(\Omega_2)$ for the energy form and preserves the $L^2$ norm ([[lem-zero-extension-from-w-one-p-zero]]), so every $k$-dimensional competitor in $H^1_0(\Omega_1)$ is a competitor in $H^1_0(\Omega_2)$ with the same Rayleigh quotient.
items.strategy: Zero extension is isometric: by [[lem-zero-extension-from-w-one-p-zero]] the extended class lies in $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^n)$ with the same component norms and derivatives equal to the zero extensions, and it belongs to $H^1_0(\Omega_2)$ because $C_c^\infty(\Omega_1)\subseteq C_c^\infty(\Omega_2)$ and the extension map is norm continuous on the closure. Since the coefficient integrals over $\Omega_2$ see only $\Omega_1$, $a^{(2)}(\widetilde u,\widetilde u)=a^{(1)}(u,u)$ and $\|\widetilde u\|_{L^2(\Omega_2)}=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega_1)}$. Apply the min-max formula of [[thm-courant-fischer-minimax-for-elliptic-eigenvalues]] to $\Omega_2$ and restrict the family of $k$-dimensional trial subspaces to the images of those in $H^1_0(\Omega_1)$: the minimum over the smaller family is at least the minimum over the larger one, giving $\lambda_k(\Omega_2)\le\lambda_k(\Omega_1)$. This is the monotonicity lemma of [Si] Lecture 10 and [LS] Theorem 10.2.

items.title: The first positive Neumann eigenvalue has the mean-zero Rayleigh characterisation
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected extension domain ([[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]), put $V:=\{u\in H^1(\Omega):\int_\Omega u=0\}$ and $L^2_0(\Omega):=\{f\in L^2(\Omega):\int_\Omega f=0\}$, and let $a(u,v)=\int_\Omega a^{ij}D_ju\overline{D_iv}\,dx$ be the principal form with Hermitian uniformly elliptic coefficients $a^{ij}=\overline{a^{ji}}$ ([[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]]); for $a^{ij}=\delta^{ij}$ this is the Neumann form of the Laplacian. Then
$$\mu_1:=\inf_{u\in V\setminus\{0\}}\frac{a(u,u)}{\|u\|^2_{L^2}}$$
satisfies $\mu_1>0$, the infimum is attained, and the minimisers are exactly the nonzero elements of the eigenspace $\{u\in V:a(u,v)=\mu_1(u,v)_{L^2}\ \forall v\in V\}$. Since both sides of that identity vanish on constants, it actually holds for every $v\in H^1(\Omega)$, so $\mu_1$ is the smallest positive weak Neumann eigenvalue on the mean-zero space and no Neumann eigenvalue of a mean-zero eigenfunction lies in $(0,\mu_1)$. Moreover $\mu_1=1/\|S\|$, where $S:L^2_0(\Omega)\to V$ is the bounded compact self-adjoint positive solution operator defined by $a(Sf,v)=(f,v)_{L^2}$ for all $v\in V$. The connectedness and extension-domain hypotheses are essential and cannot be dropped.
items.strategy: On $V$, Poincare-Wirtinger gives $\|u\|_{L^2}\le C_W\|Du\|_{L^2}$, so $a$ is coercive on $V$ with constant $\theta/(1+C_W^2)$; Lax-Milgram defines $S:L^2_0\to V$ for the bounded functional $v\mapsto(f,v)_{L^2}$. $S$ is compact (bounded into $V$, followed by the compact inclusion $V\hookrightarrow L^2_0$ supplied by the Rellich extension-domain theorem), self-adjoint and positive by the same computation as [[lem-symmetric-shifted-solution-operator-is-positive-and-self-adjoint]], and injective. Apply the compact self-adjoint spectral theorem and the expansion argument of [[lem-eigenbasis-expansion-in-the-form-norm]] with $(V,a,\mu=0)$ in place of $(H^1_0,a_\mu)$: for $u\in V$, $a(u,u)=\sum_j\mu_j|(u,e_j)|^2$, where $0<\mu_1\le\mu_2\le\cdots\to\infty$ are the reciprocals of the positive eigenvalues of $S$ and $\{e_j\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $L^2_0$; hence every quotient is at least $\mu_1$ with equality exactly on the $\mu_1$-eigenspace, and $\mu_1=1/\|S\|$. Extending the eigenequation from $V$ to $H^1(\Omega)$ uses $a(e_1,1)=0=(e_1,1)_{L^2}$; on a disconnected domain the componentwise constants would enter $V$ and the infimum would be $0$, so connectedness is essential ([L] Corollary 4.9 and the surrounding mean-zero discussion, printed pp. 95-98; [LS] Chapter 6, printed pp. 42-43; [B] Remark 30 after Theorem 9.31, printed p. 312).

items.title: The Neumann spectrum and the constant zero mode
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) and Countable Choice (CC). The explicit CC premise is used by [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]], while AC matches the cited componentwise-constancy and mean-zero Neumann results as currently stated. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded open set and let $a(u,v)=\int_\Omega a^{ij}D_ju\overline{D_iv}\,dx$ be the principal form with Hermitian uniformly elliptic coefficients ([[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]]). Then
$$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)=\int_\Omega\operatorname{Re}\big(a^{ij}D_ju\overline{D_iu}\big)dx\ge\theta\|Du\|_{L^2}^2\ge0,$$
with equality if and only if $Du=0$ a.e., i.e. if and only if $u$ is constant on each connected component of $\Omega$ ([[thm-zero-weak-gradient-implies-componentwise-constancy]]). Hence the constant functions are weak Neumann eigenfunctions with eigenvalue $0$, and on a domain with exactly $m$ connected components the zero eigenspace of the principal Neumann problem is exactly the $m$-dimensional space of componentwise constants. In particular the lowest weak Neumann eigenvalue on $H^1(\Omega)$ is $0$; a first positive eigenvalue, when it exists, lies above this zero mode. If, in addition, $\Omega$ is connected and is a Sobolev extension domain, [[thm-first-positive-neumann-eigenvalue-has-the-mean-zero-rayleigh-characterisation]] gives a positive first Neumann level after restricting to the global mean-zero subspace. This positivity conclusion is not asserted for a general bounded open $\Omega$; when $\Omega$ has multiple components, nonzero componentwise constants can also have global mean zero.
items.strategy: Under AC and CC, the inequality is pointwise ellipticity; since both integrands are nonnegative and their integrals agree, equality forces $\theta|Du|^2=0$ a.e., and the constancy statement is the published zero-gradient theorem. The weak Neumann equation $a(u,v)=0$ for all $v\in H^1(\Omega)$ is therefore satisfied by every componentwise constant and only by those, so no positive eigenvalue of the form restricted to all of $H^1$ exists. Only when $\Omega$ is also connected and a Sobolev extension domain does [[thm-first-positive-neumann-eigenvalue-has-the-mean-zero-rayleigh-characterisation]] supply a positive first level on the global mean-zero subspace; this item asserts no such positivity for a general bounded open set. ([LS] Chapter 6, printed pp. 42-43; [L] Corollary 4.9, printed p. 95; [H] Section 4.4, printed pp. 97-99).

items.title: Dirichlet Laplacian eigenpairs on an interval
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]) for the discrete-spectrum and Rayleigh-principle assertions. On \((0,\pi)\), for each integer \(k\ge1\), \(u_k(x)=\sin(kx)\) belongs to \(H^1_0(0,\pi)\) and is a weak Dirichlet eigenfunction of the positive Laplacian \(-d^2/dx^2\) with eigenvalue \(k^2\):
$$\int_0^\pi u_k'(x)\overline{v'(x)}\,dx=k^2\int_0^\pi u_k(x)\overline{v(x)}\,dx\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(0,\pi).$$
The functions \(\sin(kx)\) are pairwise \(L^2\)-orthogonal and have squared norm \(\pi/2\); hence the displayed pairs are eigenpairs with pairwise distinct eigenvalues. The Rayleigh principle gives \(\lambda_1\le1\), witnessed by \((\sin x,1)\), where \(\lambda_1\) is the first eigenvalue in [[thm-discrete-spectrum-of-a-symmetric-elliptic-dirichlet-operator]] and the variational characterization is [[thm-rayleigh-principle-for-the-first-dirichlet-eigenvalue]]. Neither completeness of \(\{\sin(kx)\}\), nor simplicity of the individual eigenvalues, nor the sharp Poincare constant is asserted here.
items.strategy:
In the coefficient convention of [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]], the coefficient choice \(a^{11}=1\), \(b=c=0\) gives the positive Laplacian and its form. The classical derivative of \(u_k\) is its weak derivative by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]], and \(u_k\in H^1\) in the norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. For \(u_k\in H^1_0(0,\pi)\), fix \(\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)\) with \(0\le\chi\le1\), \(\chi(s)=0\) for \(s\le1\), \(\chi(s)=1\) for \(s\ge2\), and bounded derivative, available from [[lem-euclidean-bump-for-a-compact-set-inside-an-open-set]]. For \(0<\varepsilon<\pi/4\), set \(\eta_\varepsilon(x)=\chi(x/\varepsilon)\chi((\pi-x)/\varepsilon)\). Then \(\eta_\varepsilon u_k\in C_c^\infty(0,\pi)\), equals \(u_k\) off the two endpoint strips of total length \(4\varepsilon\), and \(|\eta_\varepsilon'|\le C/\varepsilon\). On those strips \(|u_k'|\le k\) and \(|u_k(x)|\le k\,\operatorname{dist}(x,\{0,\pi\})\le2k\varepsilon\), using that \(k\) is an integer and \(u_k\) vanishes at both endpoints. Thus \(\|(\eta_\varepsilon-1)u_k\|_{L^2}\to0\) and
$$\|(\eta_\varepsilon u_k-u_k)'\|_{L^2}\le\|(\eta_\varepsilon-1)u_k'\|_{L^2}+\|\eta_\varepsilon'u_k\|_{L^2}\longrightarrow0,$$
so the closure definition [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]] gives \(u_k\in H^1_0(0,\pi)\). Now take any \(v\in H^1_0(0,\pi)\). By that same closure definition choose \(v_j\in C_c^\infty(0,\pi)\) with \(v_j\to v\) in \(H^1\). For each \(j\), ordinary integration by parts has no boundary term and \(u_k''=-k^2u_k\), so
$$\int_0^\pi u_k'\overline{v_j'}\,dx=-\int_0^\pi u_k''\overline{v_j}\,dx=k^2\int_0^\pi u_k\overline{v_j}\,dx.$$
The left side converges to \(\int u_k'\overline{v'}\) since its error is bounded by \(\|u_k'\|_{L^2}\|v_j'-v'\|_{L^2}\); the right side converges to \(k^2\int u_k\overline v\) with error at most \(k^2\|u_k\|_{L^2}\|v_j-v\|_{L^2}\). This proves the weak identity for every \(H^1_0\) test directly, without a dimension-restricted classical-to-weak result. The weak eigenpair definition [[def-symmetric-elliptic-weak-eigenpair]] then identifies \((k^2,u_k)\) as a Dirichlet eigenpair. For \(m\ne n\), use the product identity \(2\sin(mx)\sin(nx)=\cos((m-n)x)-\cos((m+n)x)\) from [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]] and integrate using [[thm-ftc-second-part]]; for \(m=n\), integrate \(\sin^2(nx)=(1-\cos(2nx))/2\). These give orthogonality and squared norm \(\pi/2\). The quotient for \(\sin x\) is \(\int_0^\pi|\cos x|^2dx/\int_0^\pi|\sin x|^2dx=1\), so [[thm-rayleigh-principle-for-the-first-dirichlet-eigenvalue]] gives \(\lambda_1\le1\). S: [LS] Chapter 2, one-dimensional Dirichlet spectrum, printed p. 15; [B] Section 8.6, printed pp. 231--233; [L] Exercise 4.3, printed pp. 92--93.

items.title: The Neumann Laplacian has a zero constant mode
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces. On $(0,\pi)$, the real coefficient case of the divergence-form Laplacian ([[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]]) has Neumann form $a_N(u,v)=\int_0^\pi u'v'$ on $H^1(0,\pi;\mathbb R)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). The constant function $u_0\equiv1$ satisfies $a_N(u_0,v)=0=0\cdot\int_0^\pi u_0v$ for every $v\in H^1(0,\pi;\mathbb R)$, so $(0,1)$ is a weak Neumann eigenpair ([[rem-neumann-spectrum-and-the-constant-zero-mode]]). For every integer $k\ge1$, $u_k(x)=\cos(kx)$ is a weak Neumann eigenfunction with eigenvalue $k^2$. The Neumann form is nonnegative and the constant mode has Rayleigh quotient $0$, so the lowest weak Neumann eigenvalue on $H^1(0,\pi;\mathbb R)$ is $0$. On the mean-zero subspace $\{u\in H^1(0,\pi;\mathbb R):\int_0^\pi u=0\}$ the first Rayleigh value is positive by Poincare--Wirtinger and at most $1$, witnessed by $\cos x$. The constant mode is exactly the zero mode removed by the mean-zero restriction, in contrast with the Dirichlet problem, where constants are not admissible.
items.strategy:
For $k\ge0$ put $u_k(x)=\cos(kx)$, with $u_0\equiv1$. By [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[thm-chain-rule]], $-u_k''=k^2u_k$; the quarter-turn identities in [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]] give $u_k'(0)=u_k'(\pi)=0$ (for $k=0$ this is immediate). Fix an arbitrary $v\in H^1(0,\pi;\mathbb R)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). By [[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]], its class has an absolutely continuous representative $v^*$ on $[0,\pi]$ with $(v^*)'=v'$ almost everywhere. Thus $u_k'v^*$ is absolutely continuous and $(u_k'v^*)'=u_k''v^*+u_k'v'$ almost everywhere. The fundamental theorem for absolutely continuous functions [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] and the endpoint identities yield
$$\int_0^\pi u_k'v'= [u_k'v^*]_0^\pi-\int_0^\pi u_k''v^*=k^2\int_0^\pi u_kv.$$
This is the weak Neumann identity for every $H^1$ test; no zero-trace condition is imposed on $v$, and the boundary term vanishes because the eigenfunction's normal derivative vanishes. For $k=0$ the identity reads $0=0$, giving the zero eigenvalue. For $k\ge1$, the same quarter-turn shifts give $\int_0^\pi\cos(kx)\,dx=[\sin(kx)/k]_0^\pi=0$. Poincare--Wirtinger [[thm-poincare-wirtinger-on-bounded-connected-extension-domains]] makes the Rayleigh quotient positive on the mean-zero subspace, and [[thm-first-positive-neumann-eigenvalue-has-the-mean-zero-rayleigh-characterisation]] identifies its infimum as the first positive Neumann Rayleigh value. Taking $v=u_1$ in the weak identity shows that $u_1=\cos x$ has quotient $1$, so the infimum is at most $1$. The Dirichlet comparison is the sine-eigenfunction example [[ex-dirichlet-laplacian-eigenpairs-on-an-interval]]; constants are excluded there by the zero-trace domain [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. This is the direct one-dimensional Green identity for the natural Neumann form. The cited Dirichlet classical-to-weak lemma has test class $H^1_0$ and is not used for this Neumann statement. P: integrate by parts against the absolutely continuous representative of an arbitrary $H^1$ test, keeping the Neumann boundary term explicit. S: [LS] Chapter 2, one-dimensional Neumann spectrum, printed p. 15, and Chapter 6, natural boundary conditions, printed pp. 42--43; [L] Corollary 4.9 and the mean-zero discussion, printed pp. 95--98; [B] Chapter 9 Section 9.8, Remark 30, printed p. 312.

items.title: A shift removes a negative zero-order obstruction
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, for the invoked Sobolev and interval-eigenpair suppliers; [[thm-lax-milgram]] itself requires only Countable Choice. Over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, on $\Omega=(0,\pi)$ take $Lu=-u''-10u$, so that $a(u,v)=\int_0^\pi(u'\overline{v'}-10u\overline v)\,dx$ ([[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with $a^{11}=1$, $b=0$, $c=-10$). Then $a$ is not coercive and not even nonnegative: for $u=\sin x$ one has $a(u,u)=\frac\pi2(1-10)<0$. Garding's inequality with $\theta=1$, $M_b=0$, $M_c=10$ gives
$$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\frac12\|u\|_{H^1_0}^2-\frac{21}{2}\|u\|_{L^2}^2,$$
so the shift corollary makes $a_\mu$ coercive for every $\mu\ge\frac{21}{2}$, and Lax--Milgram gives unique solvability of $-u''-10u+\mu u=f$ with zero boundary values for such $\mu$ ([[def-shifted-elliptic-solution-operator]]). Directly,
$$a_\mu(u,u)=\int_0^\pi(|u'|^2+(\mu-10)|u|^2)\,dx\ge\min(1,\mu-10)\|u\|_{H^1_0}^2.$$
Thus $a_\mu$ is coercive already for every $\mu>10$; the displayed lower bound is strictly positive when $u\ne0$, and this sharper threshold improves on the general Gårding threshold. No boundary regularity is used.
items.strategy: Test $u=\sin x$ by explicit integration: $\int_0^\pi\cos^2x\,dx=\int_0^\pi\sin^2x\,dx=\pi/2$, so $a(\sin x,\sin x)=(\pi/2)(1-10)<0$ and coercivity fails. The Gårding constants are $\alpha=1/2$ and $\beta=1/2+0+10=21/2$ by [[thm-garding-inequality-for-a-divergence-form-elliptic-operator]], and the shifted form is coercive for $\mu\ge21/2$ by [[cor-a-sufficiently-large-shift-is-coercive]]. Under the stated Countable Choice assumption, apply [[thm-lax-milgram]] to the bounded coercive form $a_\mu$ on $H^1_0(0,\pi)$ and the bounded functional $v\mapsto(f,v)_{L^2}$; this gives a unique weak solution for every $f\in L^2(0,\pi)$ at those shifts. Separately, the direct identity $a_\mu(u,u)=\|u'\|_2^2+(\mu-10)\|u\|_2^2\ge\min(1,\mu-10)(\|u'\|_2^2+\|u\|_2^2)$ proves coercivity for every $\mu>10$; its right-hand side is positive for nonzero $u$, and it gives a positive coercivity constant. The general estimate is sufficient but not sharp for this example ([H] Section 4.7 and Examples 4.14-4.15, printed pp. 100-105; [T] Section 10.2, (10.44)-(10.47), printed p. 235).

items.title: Elliptic Fredholm solvability can fail at an eigenvalue
items.statement:
Statement refuted: for the Dirichlet problem for $-\Delta$ on a bounded domain and every real datum $f\in L^2$, the equation $-\Delta u-\lambda u=f$ is uniquely solvable.
Counterexample: on $\Omega=(0,\pi)$ take the Dirichlet Laplacian and $\lambda_k=k^2$ with $k\ge1$. The homogeneous problem for $-\Delta-\lambda_k$ has the nontrivial solution $\sin(kx)$, and for $f\in L^2(0,\pi)$ the problem
$$-u''-k^2u=f,\qquad u\in H^1_0(0,\pi),$$
has a weak solution if and only if $\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(kx)\,dx=0$. In particular $f=\sin(kx)$ admits no solution, the homogeneous solution space is exactly $\operatorname{span}\{\sin(kx)\}$ (one-dimensional), and the adjoint kernel coincides with it because the operator is symmetric. Thus uniqueness fails and solvability fails exactly on the one-dimensional orthogonality condition, as the Fredholm alternative predicts.
items.strategy: The homogeneous solution space contains $\sin(kx)$ by [[ex-dirichlet-laplacian-eigenpairs-on-an-interval]] and is exactly its span: a weak solution $u\in H^1_0(0,\pi)$ of $u''+k^2u=0$ has an absolutely continuous representative with $u'\in W^{1,2}$ (the weak derivative of $u'$ is $-k^2u\in L^2$), so the ODE holds classically and the boundary values force $u=c\sin(kx)$. Since the form is symmetric, the adjoint kernel equals the homogeneous kernel; the Fredholm alternative [[thm-fredholm-alternative-for-weak-elliptic-dirichlet-problems]] then gives solvability exactly under orthogonality to $\operatorname{span}\{\sin kx\}$, and $f=\sin kx$ violates it ([H] Theorem 4.24, printed pp. 107-108; [LS] Chapter 5, resonance examples, printed pp. 33-41).

items.title: Elliptic eigenvalues need not be simple
items.strategy:
Let $\chi_\varepsilon\in C_c^\infty(0,\pi)$ satisfy $0\le\chi_\varepsilon\le1$, equal $1$ on $[2\varepsilon,\pi-2\varepsilon]$, vanish outside $[\varepsilon,\pi-\varepsilon]$, and have $|\chi_\varepsilon'|\le C/\varepsilon$. For $w=u$ or $v$, the functions $w_\varepsilon(x,y)=\chi_\varepsilon(x)\chi_\varepsilon(y)w(x,y)$ lie in $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Since each sine factor vanishes linearly at the endpoints, $w$ is $O(\varepsilon)$ on the transition strips; consequently $w_\varepsilon	o w$ and $
abla w_\varepsilon	o
abla w$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ as the strips shrink. Thus $u,v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ by its closure definition. For any $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, integration by parts has no boundary term and yields $\int
abla w\cdot\overline{
abla\varphi}=\int(-\Delta w)\overline\varphi=5\int w\overline\varphi$, because $-\Delta u=5u$ and $-\Delta v=5v$. Given arbitrary $\varphi\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, choose $\varphi_k\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $\varphi_k	o\varphi$ in $H^1$; the gradient pairing and the $L^2$ pairing are continuous in this norm, so passing to the limit proves each weak eigenidentity for every such $\varphi$. Finally, $\sin 2x=2\sin x\cos x$ and the fundamental theorem of calculus give $\int_0^\pi\sin x\sin 2x\,dx= rac23[\sin^3x]_0^\pi=0$, and similarly for the other factor. Each function is nonzero, so orthogonality implies linear independence. The discrete spectral theorem records the eigenvalues with multiplicity, and this two-dimensional eigenspace forces at least two occurrences of $5$ in the list ([LS] Chapter 2, rectangle Dirichlet spectrum, printed p. 16; [B] Section 9.8, multiplicity discussion, printed p. 311).

items.title: Coercive non-symmetric forms need not have an orthonormal eigenbasis
items.statement:
Statement refuted: every bounded coercive sesquilinear form on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.
Counterexample: on $\mathbb K^2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $a(u,v):=(Mu,v)$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]). The Hermitian part $\tfrac12(M+M^*)=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ is positive definite with smallest eigenvalue $\alpha=(3-\sqrt5)/2>0$, so $a$ is bounded and coercive with constant $\alpha$; but $M$ is not Hermitian. Its eigenvalues are $1$ and $2$, with eigenvectors $(2,-1)$ and $(1,0)$ respectively, and these are not orthogonal: $((2,-1),(1,0))=2\ne0$. Hence $a$ has no orthonormal eigenbasis in $\mathbb K^2$, although it is coercive and all its eigenvalues are real. The symmetry hypothesis of the discrete spectral theorem is therefore not redundant.
items.strategy: Compute the Hermitian part and its smallest eigenvalue: $\operatorname{Re}(Mu,u)=2|u_1|^2+2\operatorname{Re}(u_2\overline{u_1})+|u_2|^2\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$ with $\alpha=(3-\sqrt5)/2>0$. The characteristic polynomial of $M$ is $(2-\lambda)(1-\lambda)$, so the eigenvalues are $1$ and $2$; solving $(M-\lambda I)u=0$ gives the displayed eigenvectors, whose inner product is $2\ne0$. Orthonormalising them would leave the eigenspaces, and no orthonormal eigenbasis exists. This is the finite-dimensional model showing that the symmetry hypothesis of [[thm-discrete-spectrum-of-a-symmetric-elliptic-dirichlet-operator]] is load-bearing ([L] Chapter 4, Sections 4.1 and 4.4, printed pp. 83-86 and 98-100; [LS] Chapter 4, symmetry hypothesis, printed p. 27).

items.title: A coercive non-symmetric form can have non-real Galerkin eigenvalues
items.statement: On $\mathbb C^2$ let $\beta>0$, $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&\beta\\-\beta&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $a(u,v):=(Mu,v)$. Then $a$ is bounded and coercive with constant $1$, since $\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)=|u_1|^2+|u_2|^2$; but the eigenvalues of $M$ are $1\pm i\beta$, which are non-real. Consequently for every real $\lambda$ the equation $a(u,v)=\lambda(u,v)$ for all $v\in\mathbb C^2$ has no nonzero solution: this non-symmetric coercive form has no weak eigenpair at all, and its $2\times2$ Galerkin matrix has a conjugate pair of non-real eigenvalues. This shows that the reality of the eigenvalues in the discrete spectral theorem is a consequence of symmetry and not of coercivity.
items.strategy: Direct computation: $Mu=(u_1+\beta u_2,-\beta u_1+u_2)$, so $\operatorname{Re}(Mu,u)=|u_1|^2+|u_2|^2$ and $a$ is coercive with $\alpha=1$; the characteristic polynomial is $(1-\lambda)^2+\beta^2$, whose roots $1\pm i\beta$ are not real. Hence no real $\lambda$ admits a nonzero solution of $Mu=\lambda u$. The example is the two-dimensional Galerkin model that the nonsymmetric theory must avoid ([L] Chapter 4, Section 4.4, printed pp. 98-100; [LS] Chapter 4, symmetry hypothesis, printed p. 27).

items.title: A disconnected Neumann domain has a multiple zero eigenvalue
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) and Countable Choice (CC). The explicit CC premise is used by [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]], while AC matches the cited componentwise-constancy and mean-zero Neumann results as currently stated. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be the union of two disjoint open discs $B_1,B_2$ (a nonempty bounded open set with exactly two connected components), and let $a(u,v)=\int_\Omega Du\cdot\overline{Dv}\,dx$ on $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with $a^{ij}=\delta^{ij}$). Then $a(u,u)\ge0$ with equality if and only if $u$ is constant on each component, so the weak Neumann eigenvalue $0$ has the two-dimensional eigenspace
$$\{c_1\mathbf 1_{B_1}+c_2\mathbf 1_{B_2}:c_1,c_2\in\mathbb K\}.$$
The multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue equals the number of connected components. Consequently Poincare-Wirtinger with the global mean fails on $\Omega$: the mean-zero function $|B_2|\mathbf 1_{B_1}-|B_1|\mathbf 1_{B_2}$ has zero energy, so on the mean-zero subspace the Rayleigh infimum is $0$, not positive, and the connectedness hypothesis of [[thm-first-positive-neumann-eigenvalue-has-the-mean-zero-rayleigh-characterisation]] cannot be dropped.
items.strategy: Under AC and CC, the form is nonnegative by pointwise ellipticity and vanishes exactly when $Du=0$ a.e., which by the published zero-gradient theorem means $u$ is constant on each of the two components; thus the zero eigenspace is the displayed two-dimensional space. The function $|B_2|\mathbf 1_{B_1}-|B_1|\mathbf 1_{B_2}$ lies in $H^1(\Omega)$ with zero weak gradient and global mean $|B_2||B_1|-|B_1||B_2|=0$, so it belongs to the mean-zero subspace with zero Rayleigh quotient and the infimum there is $0$; connectedness is therefore needed for a positive first Neumann level ([LS] Chapter 6, printed pp. 42-43; [H] Section 4.4, printed pp. 97-99).

items.title: A repeated eigenvalue has no canonical eigenfunction basis
items.statement:
For a symmetric elliptic Dirichlet operator on a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega$, fix a weak eigenvalue $\lambda$ with eigenspace $E_\lambda$ of dimension $m\ge2$ ([[def-ltwo-operator-associated-with-a-symmetric-elliptic-form]], [[def-symmetric-elliptic-weak-eigenpair]], [[thm-discrete-spectrum-of-a-symmetric-elliptic-dirichlet-operator]]). The subspace $E_\lambda$ and the orthogonal projection $P_\lambda$ onto it are intrinsic to $L$ (and to the shifted solution operator), but no particular orthonormal basis of $E_\lambda$ is: for every unitary $U$ of the $m$-dimensional Hilbert space $E_\lambda$ the family $\{Ue_j\}$ is another orthonormal eigenbasis, and every nonzero $u\in E_\lambda$ is an eigenfunction. Consequently downstream statements must refer to $E_\lambda$, to its dimension (the multiplicity), or to $U$-invariant quantities, and never to "the" eigenfunctions of a repeated eigenvalue. This concerns only the non-canonical choice of basis, not the existence of a Hilbert basis asserted by the discrete spectral theorem.

The invariant objects are exactly the eigenspace $E_\lambda$, the orthogonal projection $P_\lambda$ onto it, and the multiplicity $\dim E_\lambda$, which is finite by [[thm-discrete-spectrum-of-a-symmetric-elliptic-dirichlet-operator]]; the eigenfunctions themselves are $L^2$ classes, and no canonical representative of a class is selected either ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The remark records a convention for downstream statements; it proves nothing beyond linear algebra inside the finite-dimensional space $E_\lambda$.
items.strategy: Eigenfunctions of $\lambda$ form the linear subspace $E_\lambda$, which is invariant under every unitary of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space $E_\lambda$; applying such a unitary to an orthonormal basis preserves orthonormality and the eigenfunction property, so the basis is not determined by $L$. The eigenspace and its orthogonal projection are the invariant objects, and the multiplicity $\dim E_\lambda$ is finite by the discrete spectral theorem. No proof beyond linear algebra in $E_\lambda$ is required, and no canonical basis is constructed ([Si] Lecture 10, printed p. 100; [LS] Chapter 9, printed pp. 51-56).

items.title: The resolvent norm blows up at an eigenvalue
items.statement:
Assume the setting of [[cor-noninvertible-elliptic-shifts-form-a-discrete-set-in-the-self-adjoint-case]] and let $(\lambda_k,e_k)$ be a weak eigenpair with $\|e_k\|_{L^2}=1$ ([[def-symmetric-elliptic-weak-eigenpair]]). Then for every real $\lambda\notin\{\lambda_j\}$
$$\|(L-\lambda)^{-1}\|\ \ge\ \frac1{|\lambda_k-\lambda|},$$
because $(L-\lambda)^{-1}e_k=e_k/(\lambda_k-\lambda)$ has $L^2$ norm $1/|\lambda_k-\lambda|$; combined with the exact formula of the spectral-series corollary this gives $\|(L-\lambda)^{-1}\|=1/\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\{\lambda_j\})$. Hence the resolvent norm is unbounded on every neighbourhood of an eigenvalue: at $\lambda=\lambda_k-\varepsilon$ it is at least $1/\varepsilon$. The Fredholm alternative is consistent with this: at $\lambda=\lambda_k$ the homogeneous problem has the nonzero solution $e_k$, and uniqueness and bounded invertibility both fail.
items.strategy: The identity $(L-\lambda)e_k=(\lambda_k-\lambda)e_k$ (from the weak eigenequation and the definition of $D(L)$) gives $(L-\lambda)^{-1}e_k=e_k/(\lambda_k-\lambda)$ for $\lambda\notin\{\lambda_j\}$; taking $L^2$ norms and using $\|e_k\|=1$ yields the lower bound for the operator norm. Equality with $1/\operatorname{dist}$ and unboundedness near each eigenvalue are immediate from the spectral-series formula; the failure at $\lambda=\lambda_k$ is the Fredholm alternative statement ([H] Section 4.10, printed pp. 109-110; [Si] Lecture 10, printed pp. 105-107).
